summary:
AfterLight is a cloud-native, GPU-accelerated web platform that transforms complex SPHEREx infrared survey data into an interactive tool for discovering moving, faint, and variable astronomical objects. SPHEREx observes the entire sky across 102 near-infrared bands, but its Linear Variable Filters cause wavelength to vary between observations, making conventional image blinking unreliable for detecting real motion.

Our solution uses temporal difference imaging to suppress stationary stars and reveal moving objects as distinctive dipoles, while motion vectors and real-time 102-band spectral extraction provide additional evidence for candidate identification. The platform also integrates Gaia DR3 and WISE/NEOWISE data to validate motion and extend the observational baseline. Molecular templates for methane, water, and carbon monoxide help users investigate the spectral characteristics of cold astronomical objects.

By performing visualization and processing directly in the browser using WebGL2, AfterLight reduces the need for specialized astronomical software and makes large-scale infrared data more accessible to researchers and citizen scientists. Its goal is to turn complex NASA data into an intuitive discovery workflow that can help uncover objects hidden within massive astronomical surveys.
details:
AfterLight is a browser-based astronomical discovery platform designed to make SPHEREx’s complex time-domain infrared data easier to analyze and explore.

The system processes SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images and multi-epoch observations, where the Linear Variable Filter causes wavelength to vary across the detector. Instead of relying on conventional image blinking, AfterLight uses temporal difference imaging to suppress stationary sources and reveal moving objects as distinctive dipole signatures.

The platform combines several processing and visualization techniques, including 6-detector array co-addition, zodiacal-light subtraction, artifact and quality-flag masking, dynamic contrast enhancement, sub-pixel motion estimation, and real-time extraction of 102-band infrared spectra. Users can also compare observations with Gaia DR3 and historical WISE/NEOWISE data to validate motion and extend the temporal baseline. Molecular templates for methane (CH₄), carbon monoxide (CO), and water (H₂O) provide additional spectral clues for identifying cold brown dwarfs, planetary objects, and other infrared sources.

A major benefit is accessibility. AfterLight performs visualization and image-processing operations directly in the browser using WebGL2, reducing dependence on specialized astronomical software, local installations, or continuous server-side computation. This makes the platform suitable for researchers as well as citizen scientists who may not have experience working with FITS files, coordinate transformations, or astronomical data pipelines.

The intended impact is to reduce the gap between massive astronomical datasets and human discovery. By converting difficult-to-interpret infrared observations into interactive difference images, motion vectors, and spectral fingerprints, AfterLight can help users identify faint moving or variable objects more efficiently and investigate potential discoveries.

The project was developed as a software-only solution using web technologies, WebGL2 GPU processing, astronomical data formats and standards such as FITS, Astropy-based coordinate handling, and integrations with NASA SPHEREx data, Gaia DR3, WISE/NEOWISE, VizieR, and astronomical catalogs. The architecture uses cloud-native data access and client-side processing to support scalable exploration without requiring dedicated hardware.

Our creative approach was to treat SPHEREx data as a 4D spatio-spectral discovery problem, combining space, time, wavelength, and motion into one interactive interface. We specifically considered SPHEREx’s instrument characteristics, the enormous scale of the dataset, faint-object visibility, spectral variation between observations, computational efficiency, scientific validation, usability for non-experts, and future scalability.

The result is AfterLight — a platform that turns complex infrared survey data into a visual and interactive workflow for discovering and understanding objects across the sky.
